what: The engine's force error at the configuration the acceptance thresholds are defined at, so it is comparable with them for the first time.
host: Apple M3 Pro, macOS 14, Google Chrome 155, apple · metal-3
protocol: tools/calibrate_thresholds.py's own equilibration, saved with --save-equilibrated so every engine sees the same coordinates: minimise to 10 kJ/mol/nm over at most 10000 iterations, setVelocitiesToTemperature(298 K, seed 1234), then 5000 steps of LangevinIntegrator(298 K, 1/ps, 2 fs) with a 1e-6 constraint tolerance and seed 1234. Equilibration is stochastic, which is why the state is saved rather than re-run.

force_relative_rms._definition: sqrt(sum((a-b)^2) / sum(b^2)) over all 3N components; identical formula in src/gpu/verify.ts and tools/calibrate_thresholds.py, which is what makes these comparable

total_energy.note: The asymmetry is real and is not a defect: the engine's forces beat OpenMM's single-precision platform by 12.9x while its total energy is about twice as far out. Forces accumulate exactly in 64-bit fixed point, whereas the total is a difference of two large cancelling PME terms (+122000 and -154000 kJ/mol here), so its relative error is amplified by the cancellation rather than by the accumulator.

reference_cross_check.note: Independent confirmation that the two double-precision references are interchangeable, which is what makes the force comparison legitimate at all: each engine is measured against its own f64 reference. The cross-feed in test/crossfeed.test.ts gave 9.2e-12 on a different system; this is the same claim at the configuration actually used here.

verdict: The engine is inside the basis by a wide margin on forces -- 1.10e-06 against the 1.43e-05 threshold -- and sits nearer OpenMM's double-precision CPU platform (8.67e-07) than its single-precision GPU one. That is the designed consequence of 64-bit fixed-point positions and exact force accumulation; the only single-precision step is the per-pair evaluation itself.
